title: Polymer matrix drives thermal stimulation-caused dynamic phosphorescence in dispersed chromophores

paper_content.abstract: Polymer matrix has been extensively explored for decades to achieve efficient room-temperature phosphorescence from dispersed chromophores. However, the impact of the polymer matrix on the optical characteristics of chromophores remains elusive. Herein, we report that different asymmetric environments of polymer matrix delicately regulate the thermally stimulated phosphorescence property (estimated maximum total Φ : 92% at 298 K) of the molecularly dispersed chromophores. It essentially controls the degree of exo- and endothermic transition of excited states with the same and different multiplicity. The excited-state calculations demonstrate a significant influence of matrix environment on the dynamic phosphorescence property. Furthermore, we have investigated the impact of matrix-assisted conformers on dynamic phosphorescence for BANHPh and BANMePh in contrast to the completely locked geometry of BANH2. These matrix-induced, tunable phosphorescent emitters have been found to be highly competent in applications such as information encryption and afterglow display.

However, the intriguing chemistry of dynamic phosphorescence, induced by a thermal stimulation effect, in a molecularly dispersed system within a matrix environment, has remained unexplored and unclear. Our group has been actively involved in developing organic RTP systems derived from the molecular dispersion of chromophores in Poly(methyl methacrylate) (PMMA) matrix. As part of the ongoing program, we set out to investigate the impact of the asymmetric environment created by the PMMA matrix on analyzing the credible origin of thermal stimulation-caused dynamic phosphorescence properties in purely organic and economically efficient molecularly dispersed systems.

In this work, we have selected metal-free borylaniline derivatives, comprising the amine donor and -BMes acceptor, as model compounds. Accordingly, BANH2 with efficient donor-acceptor property has been rationally designed with a locked geometry to suppress unwanted molecular motions. Moreover, BANHPh and BANMePh have also been analyzed to verify the influence of conformational change on the dynamic phosphorescence property. These chromophores are strategically allowed for conformational freedom only to the N-C(xylyl) group with locked geometry around the boron center (Fig. 1a). The temperature-dependent PL experiment indicates an excellent TSDP feature of PMMA matrix emitters due to the optimal energy gap of close-lying triplet states (ΔETT: 130 meV‒230 meV) of dispersed chromophores. The side-chain ester and α-methyl group-containing PMMA has been found to be a suitable matrix for the dispersed chromophores to efficiently utilize the up-converted excitons under thermal stimulation (Fig. 1a‒b). Thereafter, a theoretical investigation further reveals the importance of the matrix environment on the dynamic phosphorescence of the isolated chromophores, relative to calculations in the gaseous phase. In addition, we observe an intriguing finding where the matrix environment could lift the degeneracy of the conformers in the T1 state by providing an asymmetric environment, which is not likely to occur in the absence of matrix surroundings. These emitters are successfully explored for anticounterfeiting applications and promising afterglow materials.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_1:
In this manuscript, the authors designed and synthesized three borylaniline derivatives, which were found to show dual persistent emissions in PMMA matrix. After experimental and theoretical and experimental studies, the authors ascribed this to the existence of two conformers within T1 state (T1H and T1L) with the assistance of PMMA matrix. The luminescent phenomena reported in this work are interesting, but the internal mechanism should be further clarified before its publication.
1. In this work, the persistent emission (@450 nm) at room temperature seems to be from TADF, science it is almost overlapped with the steady-state PL spectra. In previous literatures, such as Sci. China Chem. 2023, 66, 1120 and Chem. Mater. 2024, 36, 3000, the similar phenomena have been reported.
2. Compounds BANHPh and BANMePh with asymmetrical structure could present conformational isomerism, which might show dual phosphorescence emissions from two different conformers. However, BANH2 with symmetrical structure also showed dual persistent emissions, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 25. The authors should clarify this point.
3. As shown in Figure 6h, several stable conformers were presented in the relaxed potential energy scans of T1 state. Then, could the emission peaks be calculated for these T1 conformers to compare with those in experimental results? How about the potential energy scans of T1 state for compound BANH2?

Comments
In the current report, Thilagar and Co-workers presented the dual phosphorescence behaviour of the borylaniline derivatives in the PMMA matrix. The presented organic chromophores show dual delayed emission behaviour under deaerated conditions, which is interesting in the field of triplet photophysics. However, authors have explained that the dual delayed emission phenomenon arises from the matrix-assisted, room-temperature accessible conformers within the T1 state via a thermally stimulated delayed phosphorescence mechanism, which may not be accurate. Thus, the current version of the manuscript requires proper justification of fundamental photophysical analysis and an explanation of the mechanism involved with proper experimental support, which is missing. Many experimental data, especially dual delayed emission behaviour, need reinvestigation with appropriate care. Hence, the present work requires major revisions for publication in a high-quality journal like Nature Communications. Moreover, the authors should address all the points raised below.
1. Change in the dihedral angle at 100 K and 300 K is relatively low (negligible changes) in the single crystal data. However, the authors have concluded that dual emission arises from matrix-assisted, room-temperature accessible conformers within the T1 state. The authors should reinvestigate the mechanism using proper experimental data. What is the photophysics of the molecules in the crystalline state? The authors should do a detailed investigation.
2. The asymmetric environment in the PMMA matrix could be due to the aggregation propensity of the chromophores, and 1 wt% chromophore doping may not prevent the aggregation. The authors should perform a wt% dependent study from 0.1% to 10 % and should take their delayed spectra and compare them. It might happen that authors are seeing phosphorescence from the monomeric and aggregated state of the chromophores. Please see one of the examples: https://doi.org/10.1002/anie.202101538
3. Authors should experimentally find the original triplet state of the presented chromophores in a dilute solution state at cryogenic temperature.
4. 'The rigid polymer (PMMA) matrix eliminates the possibility of vibrational relaxation-caused quenching of excited state species. Time-gated PL measurement of 1 wt.% BANHPh@PMMA (50 μs delay time) at room temperature showed a structureless broad emission band at 450 nm (Fig. 2a).' what about the role of oxygen? The authors presented all the observations in the PMMA matrix under oxygen-free conditions (according to Figure S21). The authors should mention it clearly. Harnessing triplet exciton under ambient conditions is always more important than oxygen-free conditions. The authors should clarify and present the observations, which should be very clear to the readers.
5. 'The delayed emission band (λ = 450 nm) was slightly lower in energy than the prompt emission band (λ = 445 nm), as depicted in Fig. 2a and 2h.' The shift could be due to the change in the excited state geometry of the chromophores due their CT nature in the excited state. Please see also the other example: https://doi.org/10.1038/nphoton.2012.31.
6. Page 5, lines 195-196: 'Moreover, the strong oxygen sensitivity and faster decay of delayed emission at elevated temperatures featured the possibility of RTP rather than TADF (Fig. 2d and Supplementary Fig. 24, 26).' In my opinion, this statement is incorrect without adequate experimental support.
7. Suppose I claim that the high energy emission band is a delayed fluorescence band either by thermal activation derived or triplet fusion-induced delayed fluorescence emission; what extra experimental support author will present that my claim is wrong (or right)?
8. In SI line 582, 'Fluorescence quantum yield was determined with an integrating sphere under ambient conditions. The total photoluminescence quantum yield and phosphorescence quantum yield were obtained by following the previous literatures.' According to the SI figure S21, the authors do not have a triplet contribution to the total emission under ambient conditions; how did the authors calculate the total QY under vacuum? Please show all quantum yield measurement spectra (snapshot) under air and vacuum and the phosphorescence quantum yield measurement. Also, show a snapshot, justify how authors measured the quantum yield at 77 K, and adequately write instruments and methods in the SI.
9. Please explain and show detailed temperature dependence for two bands of all the chromophores for all the temperatures from 77 K to 298 K, not only from 225 K to 298 K) because the conclusion drawn from the temperature-dependent lifetime decay profile is unsatisfactory.
10. Page 3, line 111 'We observe an extraordinary finding': Please refrain from an objective like this.
11. Authors should check 'photo physics' throughout the manuscript appropriately.
12. Authors should cite more appropriate literature where the organic chromophores show dual delayed emission (either dual phosphorescence or delayed fluorescence and phosphorescence).
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Subhajit Ghosh et al. analyzed the dual phosphorescence behavior of three chromophores molecularly dispersed (1 wt.% concentration) in the PMMA matrix. They employed second-order Algebraic Diagrammatic Construction (ADC2) excited state calculations to show that the dual phosphorescence observed in BANHPh and BANMePh does not stem from the T1 and T2 electronic states. Instead, this phenomenon arises from matrix-assisted, room-temperature accessible conformers within the T1 state (T1Hand T1L). In conclusion, conformation-dependent dual phosphorescence is unlikely to occur without the PMMA matrix. The present results can be utilized for temperature sensing from the ratiometric phosphorescence afterglow colour change-over in a short energy range. In this sense, I suggest that this work can be accepted after addressing the following concerns.
1.What is the behaviour of phosphorescence when the mass concentration is between 1wt.% and 10wt.%?
2.Is the dual phosphorescence behaviour similar in other polymer matrices besides PMMA and PBMA?
3.Please note the uniform format of the paper, like “ADC(2)” and “ADC2”, and “T1/T2-S1 andT1/T2-S0” on page 9.
4.Some typical recently literatures about long-lifetime RTP should be cited, such as 10.1038/s41467-024-47378-2; 10.1038/s41467-023-43133-1; 10.1021/jacs.2c02076； 10.1002/adma.202416397；10.1002/ange.202411323, et al.
5.Please note the normality of the figures, like Fig. 1c.

Response: We thank the reviewer for the appreciating our effort on the work. We have re-investigated the photophysical behaviour of the chromophores at 0.1 wt.% concentration in three different matrices (PMMA, PBMA, and PS) with variable electronic and steric environment to understand the internal mechanism of the dynamic dual phosphorescence. Please see the text in page 14-16 of manuscript for detailed mechanistic insights.
NB:
• We have opted to change the phrase ‘dual phosphorescence’ to ‘dynamic phosphorescence’ by considering the presence of multiple triplet excited state for the temperature-dependent studies.
• The thermally stimulated delayed emission phenomenon has also been highlighted in the manuscript since matrix plays an important role to control the thermal stimulation effect on delayed emission band. The title of the current work has been modified from “Polymer Matrix Drives Dual Phosphorescence in Dispersed Chromophores” to “Polymer Matrix Drives Thermal Stimulation-Caused Dynamic Phosphorescence in Dispersed Chromophores” to highlight the matrix-driven thermal stimulation effect on the dynamic delayed emission property.
Comment 1: In this work, the persistent emission (@450 nm) at room temperature seems to be from TADF, science it is almost overlapped with the steady-state PL spectra. In previous literatures, such as Sci. China Chem. 2023, 66, 1120 and Chem. Mater. 2024, 36, 3000, the similar phenomena have been reported.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment and sharing the related references. According to reviewer’s suggestion we have re-investigated the emission process.
(a) The steady-state emission spectra and delayed emission spectra are almost overlapping. However, the distinct spectral nature of the prompt and delayed emission bands—specifically, the delayed emission's feeble vibrational feature (lower energy end) which is absent in the fluorescence band (recorded in presence of O2) infers different nature of the delayed emission band (Fig. 3b and Supplementary Figs. 23).
(b) We have recorded the steady-state emission spectra under vacuum and in presence of O2 to distinguish the nature of the delayed emission (TADF or RTP), although it is difficult to realize the presence of triple excited state closely lying to S1 state. The steady-state emission band under vacuum condition is combination of fluorescence band and delayed emission band. On the other hand, delayed emission band is quenching in presence of oxygen and therefore, steady-state emission band exhibited an attenuated spectral area in presence of O2. Interestingly, normalization of spectra exhibited that there is a small blue-shift in spectral maxima for the steady-state emission band in presence of O2 with reduced fwhm value relative to spectrum under vacuum (Supplementary Figs. 45-47). This clearly indicates the presence of triplet excited state energetically close to singlet excited state and negates the possibility of solely TADF phenomenon for delayed emission band.
Please see the related reference. https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c02930
(c) We have also re-examined the tail-fitting of lifetime decay profile for the delayed emission maxima. The lifetime decay is found to exhibit a tri-exponential decay kinetics without compromising the shorter time range during fitting. For bi-exponential fitting, the shorter time range typically needs to be excluded (previous version of manuscript); however, this would not be suitable for this phenomenon. The O2-sensitive spectra behaviour and temperature dependent variation of amplitude percentage of three delayed component concludes that the delayed emission band at 298 K is a combination of higher energy phosphorescence (HEP) band, lower energy phosphorescence (LEP) band and a modest contribution of thermally activated delayed fluorescence (TADF) considering the spectral overlap of prompt and delayed emission band. Please see the text in page 5-7 of manuscript and Supplementary Tables 11-13, 15-17, 19-21 for detailed information.
Please see the related reference. https://doi.org/10.1021/jacs.4c02930

The snapshots of the lifetime decay profile are provided showing tri-exponential, bi-exponential and mono-exponential fitting of decay (Supplementary Figs. 45-47).

However, BANH2 with symmetrical structure also showed dual persistent emissions, as shown in Supplementary Fig. 25. The authors should clarify this point.
Response: We thank the reviewer for the comment. We have justified the dynamic dual phosphorescence for the emitters based on experimental support in addition to theoretical calculations as following.
We would also like to point out that our wavefunction-based ADC(2) calculations reveal a slightly higher T2–T1 gap in BANHPh@PMMA and BANMePh@PMMA compared to BANH2@PMMA, supporting the argument that the T2 state might be involved in the dual phosphorescence observed in BANH2 (see Fig. 4). “BANH2 demonstrates relatively higher k nr / k r value (>1) compared to other two chromophores even in PMMA matrix (despite the temperature dependent PL integral suggesting a less likely non-radiative pathway). This signifies a higher degree of intersystem crossing (ISC) between singlet excited state (S1) and triplet excited states for BANH2. For BANHPh and BANMePh, intersystem crossing (ISC) to the T2 state is possible. Please see the text in page 14-16 of manuscript for detailed information.

Author’s response to previous comment 1 and new comment 1 (Photophysics in crystalline state):
We thank the reviewer for the careful reassessment and for highlighting the need to clearly distinguish the origin of delayed emission in the crystalline state from that observed for isolated chromophores in a PMMA matrix.
The delayed emission band observed between 400 and 475 nm at a delay time of 50 μs in the crystalline state (Figure 2f; Supplementary Figures S27 and S28) does not correspond to phosphorescence analogous to the low-energy or high-energy phosphorescence bands observed in PMMA. Instead, this band is assigned to delayed fluorescence, which coexists with a lower-energy phosphorescence band appearing at wavelengths above 500 nm.
This assignment is supported by several experimental observations. First, the higher-energy delayed band in the crystalline state spectrally overlaps with the prompt fluorescence, indicating a singlet origin. The peak maxima of this band lie in the range of 445–462 nm for all crystalline samples, whereas the phosphorescence band is consistently red-shifted (> 500 nm). As a result, emission in the 400–475 nm range cannot be attributed to phosphorescence in the crystalline phase.
Second, the phosphorescence observed in the crystalline state differs substantially from that of discrete chromophores in PMMA. The crystalline-state phosphorescence is red-shifted and exhibits shorter lifetimes than both the LEP and HEP bands in PMMA (Figure 2f; Supplementary Figures 34a–e). Moreover, the temperature dependence and temporal evolution of the delayed emission spectra differ qualitatively between the two environments, indicating distinct emissive mechanisms.
Structural analysis further supports this distinction. Single-crystal data reveal a face-to-face antiparallel molecular arrangement; however, the centroid-to-centroid distances between xylyl rings (8.2 Å for BANHPh, 7.2 Å for BANMePh, and 5.9 Å for BANH2) are too large to support significant π–π stacking or H-aggregate formation in the ground state. In addition, the angles between the B–xylyl–N plane and the centroid-connecting axis (121.5°, 32.1°, and 91°, respectively) disfavour efficient orbital overlap.
Consistent with this interpretation, excitation spectra of the crystalline samples exhibit a bathochromic shift relative to those of discrete chromophores in PMMA (Supplementary Figures 34f–h), indicating intermolecular stabilization of the excited states in the solid phase. We therefore attribute the red-shifted emission and altered decay dynamics in the crystalline state to intermolecularly modified excited-state energetics, rather than to the matrix-assisted triplet states' energetics responsible for dual phosphorescence in PMMA.

In addition, the supplementary figure 11 has been updated with additional figures demonstrating intermolecular distances in crystal packing. Supplementary Figure 34 is added to compare the steady-state and time-gated spectra of the crystalline state and dispersed state in the PMMA matrix.

The ns-TA measurements further confirm that the long-lived absorption in the 420–520 nm region corresponds to the T1 state, with microsecond lifetimes.
